'''Frank Asaro''' (born Francesco Asaro, July 31, 1927 – June 10, 2014) was an Emeritus Senior Scientist at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] associated with the [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California at Berkeley]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Francesco "Frank" Asaro Obituary|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/contracostatimes/obituary.aspx?pid=171387011|accessdate=8 June 2015|agency=Contra Costa Times|date=18 June 2014}}</ref> He is best known as the chemist who discovered the [[iridium anomaly]] in the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary]] layer that led the team of [[Luis Walter Alvarez|Luis Alvarez]], [[Walter Alvarez]], Frank Asaro, and [[Helen Vaughn Michel|Helen Michel]] to propose the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event|Asteroid-Impact Theory]], which postulates that an asteroid hit the Earth sixty-five million years ago and caused mass extinction during the age of the dinosaurs.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Frank Asaro, Nuclear Chemist Who Contributed to Dinosaur Extinction Theory and Archaeological Studies, Passes Away | author1= Allan Chen| author2= David Adan-Bayewitz|url=https://eta.lbl.gov/news/57850/frank-asaro-nuclear-chemist-who|access-date=2023-01-02|website=Berkeley Lab | date=June 16, 2014}}</ref>

==Biography==
Asaro grew up in [[Escondido, California]], the son of [[avocado]] farmer and barber Nicolo Asaro and Antonina (Annie) Asaro.  He married Lucille Marie Lavezo and settled in the California Bay Area. They had four children, Frank, Antonina, [[Catherine Asaro|Catherine]], and Marianna.  Asaro's mother, one of the oldest known residents of Escondido, lived until almost 106 years old.<ref>{{Cite web|author1=Tom Pfingsten | agency= The North County Times|date=2010-12-08|title=IN PERSON:105-year-old birthday girl reveals longevity's secret: blackjack |url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/sdut-in-person105-year-old-birthday-girl-reveals-2010dec08-story.html|access-date=2023-01-02|website=San Diego Union-Tribune|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Research==
===The Early Berkeley Years===
Asaro went to college at age sixteen during World War II and earned both his undergraduate and Ph.D. degrees in chemistry from the [[University of California, Berkeley]].  For his doctorate, he worked with Professor [[Isadore Perlman]] on alpha decay processes in nuclear chemistry.<ref name=Perlman>{{Citation
| url = https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/perlman-isadore.pdf
| title = Isadore Perlman: 1915–1991 – A Biographical Memoir
| author1= Glenn T. Seaborg
| author1-link= Glenn T. Seaborg
| author2= Frank Asaro
| date= 1998
| publisher= National Academies Press
| place= Washington DC
}}</ref>{{rp|13}} Asaro and Perlman collaborated over the next fourteen years on studies of nuclear structure.  It was during this time that they developed a high-precision technique of [[neutron activation analysis]] that has become a standard for determining the origin of ancient artifacts, in particular pottery.<ref>{{ cite web
| url-status= dead | url=http://archaeometry.missouri.edu/datasets/lbnl/index.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080409015316/http://archaeometry.missouri.edu/datasets/lbnl/index.html |archive-date=2008-04-09
| title= Introduction to the LBNL Nuclear Archaeology Database
| date= 10 March 2008
| author1= Archaeometry Lab
| publisher=University of Missouri-Columbia Research Center
| work=Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory Nuclear Archaeology Database}}</ref> Asaro initially agreed to work on the project for a few months.  He later wrote, "How good was Perlman at choosing new fields? I thought I would take three months off to do this. I made that decision in 1967, and I'm still doing this work 32 years later."<ref name=NuclearPhysics>{{ cite web
| author1= Allen Chen | date = December 1999
| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20001019110949/http://www.lbl.gov/Science-Articles/Archive/nuclear-archaeology.html
| archive-date= 19 October 2000
| url-status=dead
| url =http://www.lbl.gov/Science-Articles/Archive/nuclear-archaeology.html | title=Nuclear Physics Sheds Light on Ancient Archeological Mysteries
| work = Berkeley Lab}}</ref>

One of the first projects Asaro tackled with Perlman was a study of ancient pottery from Cyprus, known as [[Cypriot Bichrome ware]]. Aided by the Swedish archaeologist [[Einar Gjerstad]], they obtained 1,200 pottery sherds from the second millennium BCE excavated by the [[Swedish Cyprus Expedition]] in 1927–1931.  Among the many results of those studies was the work done with Michal Artzy, a then graduate student at [[Brandeis University|Brandeis]]. Up until that time, a distinctive type pottery called "Bichrome Ware", first found in Tel Ajjul in [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]] by the archaeologist [[Sir Flinders Petrie]], was believed to originate in Palestine after which it was exported to sites in the eastern [[Mediterranean]]. Thrown on a fast wheel and painted with animals and birds, the unusual pottery appeared to be the work of a new painter or school of painting. The Berkeley group showed that in fact the chemical composition of the pieces matched that of pottery made in [[Cyprus]], which meant it had later been exported to Palestine and other sites, a result that had extensive ramifications on the archaeology of the eastern Mediterranean.<ref name=Perlman />{{rp|15–16}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Artzy |first1=Michal |last2=Asaro |first2=Frank |last3=Perlman |first3=Isadore | author3-link = Isadore Perlman |date=1973 |title=The Origin of the "Palestinian" Bichrome Ware |publisher =University of Michigan Press  |journal=Journal of the American Oriental Society |volume=93 |issue=4 |pages=446–461 |doi=10.2307/600164 |issn=0003-0279 | jstor= 600164}}</ref>

===The Colossi of Memnon===

In 1973, Asaro and his colleagues embarked on a study of the [[Colossi of Memnon]], two statues of Pharaoh Amenhotep III that have stood for 3400 years in the Theban necropolis, across the River [[Nile]] from the modern city of [[Luxor]].  Collaborating with Professor [[Robert Heizer]] and his research group in the Department of Anthropology and Archaeological Research at the University of California, Berkeley, the Asaro group analyzed the stone used to construct the statues.  Erected in the early 14th century BCE as guardians of the [[Mortuary Temple]], the two 50-foot monoliths consist of a quartzose sandstone rock ([[quartzite]]) formed by quartz particles cemented with iron oxide.  Archeologists had once believed that all the stone used to create the statues came from a quarry about {{cvt|100|miles|km}} away from the temple site, near [[Aswan]]. Asaro's group determined that the original rock used to build the statues actually came from quarries 420 miles away in [[Cairo]], [[Egypt]] and was transported overland to the final site, a remarkable feat of engineering for that time. Using neutron activation analysis, Asaro and his co-workers showed that the stone from Aswan was only used to repair the upper half of the northern statue, which had been knocked over in an earthquake about 27 {{sc|bce}} and reconstructed by Roman emperor [[Septimius Severus]] about {{nowrap|197 CE}}.<ref name = NuclearPhysics /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Heizer |first1=R. F. |last2=Stross |first2=F. |last3=Hester |first3=T. R. |last4=Albee |first4=A. |last5=Perlman |first5=Isadore |last6=Asaro |first6=Frank |last7=Bowman |first7=H. |date=21 December 1973|title=The Colossi of Memnon Revisited: Recent research has established the source of the stone of the two 720-ton statues at Thebes. |jstor= 1737557 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=182 |issue=4118 |pages=1219–1225 |doi=10.1126/science.182.4118.1219 |pmid=17811309 |s2cid=39052980 |issn=0036-8075}}</ref>

===The Plate of Brass===

The Plate of Brass, also known as [[Drake's Plate of Brass|Drake's Plate]], is an artifact that English explorer [[Francis Drake]] purportedly left on the coast of what is now Marin County, in the San Francisco Bay Area of California, after his ship the [[Golden Hinde]] landed there in 1579. However, in 1977, Asaro and his colleague Helen Michel used neutron activation analysis to determine that the zinc content in the composition of the plate was too high and the impurity levels too low to come from techniques of sixteenth century English for working with brass.  Instead, the plate was mostly likely manufactured in the first half of the nineteenth century or later.<ref>{{Cite web
| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20060615082011/http://www.lbl.gov/Science-Articles/Archive/NSD-Drakes-plate.html
| author1= Allen Chen| url-status= dead
| date= 4 April 2003
| archive-date= 15 June 2006
| work = Berkeley Lab
| url=http://www.lbl.gov/Science-Articles/Archive/NSD-Drakes-plate.html|title=Drake's Plate -- the end of the mystery?}}</ref><ref>{{ cite book | title=Scientific Investigation of Copies, Fakes and Forgeries| editor1= Paul Craddock| place=Oxford|publisher= Butterworth-Heinemann|date= 2009| isbn= 978-0-7506-4205-7}}</ref>{{page needed|date= July 2023}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Michel |first1=Helen V. |last2=Asaro |first2=Frank |date=February 1979 |title=Chemical Study of the Plate of Brass |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1475-4754.1979.tb00237.x |journal=Archaeometry |publisher= Wiley Blackwell |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=3–19 |doi=10.1111/j.1475-4754.1979.tb00237.x |bibcode=1979Archa..21....3M |issn=0003-813X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===The Asteroid Impact Theory===

Asaro is best known as the nuclear chemist who discovered the [[iridium anomaly]] that led to the development of the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event|asteroid impact theory]] to explain the mass extinctions, including the demise of the dinosaurs, that occurred at the end of the geological era known as the [[Cretaceous]] period in Earth's history.<ref name=DinoPaper>{{Cite journal |last1=Alvarez |first1=Luis W.
|author1-link= Luis Walter Alvarez |last2=Alvarez |first2=Walter | author2-link = Walter Alvarez
|last3=Asaro |first3=Frank |last4=Michel |first4=Helen V. |date=6 June 1980 |title=Extraterrestrial Cause for the Cretaceous-Tertiary Extinction |url=http://www3.geosc.psu.edu/~jfk4/Geosci_500/Discussion%20papers/Alvarez_etal_Science_80.pdf |journal=Science |language=en |volume=208 |issue=4448 |pages=1095–1108 | jstor = 1683699 |doi=10.1126/science.208.4448.1095 |pmid=17783054
|bibcode=1980Sci...208.1095A
|s2cid=16017767
|issn=0036-8075|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021042738/http://www3.geosc.psu.edu/~jfk4/Geosci_500/Discussion%20papers/Alvarez_etal_Science_80.pdf
|archive-date=2012-10-21
}}</ref>  His part in the work began when [[Nobel Prize]]–winning physicist [[Luis Walter Alvarez|Luis Alvarez]] and his son, geologist [[Walter Alvarez]], asked Asaro to look for iridium in samples of earth from the layer between the Cretaceous and [[Paleogene]] periods.  Their purpose was to discover if the composition of the boundary layer that represented the transition between those two periods could provide insight into how many years the layer represented.

Asaro told the Alvarezes that the amount of iridium present in such samples of the Earth would almost certainly be too small to detect.  However, he was interested in the project and agreed to perform the analysis, working with colleague Helen Michel.  When they discovered remarkably high levels of iridium, he believed they had done the analysis incorrectly.  He and Michel repeated the tests many times before bringing their results to Alvarez. Walter Alvarez has written, "Frank hunts down potential mistakes with the ruthlessness of a counterspy, triple checks everything, and then checks it again .... We know today what killed the dinosaurs because of Frank Asaro's ability to make these remarkable measurements."<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kkHhl67ixwEC | title=T. Rex and the Crater of Doom | publisher=Princeton University Press | author=Alvarez, Walter | orig-year=1997| year=2008| pages=67–68 | isbn=9780691131030}}</ref> The results were soon confirmed, not only for the samples provided by Alvarez, but independently by other groups around the world. That discovery resulted in the group, led by Luis Alvarez, to propose that an asteroid collided with the Earth and caused the mass extinctions.<ref name=DinoPaper />  Although the theory is sometimes referred to as the [[Alvarez hypothesis]], the seminal paper published in the literature was authored by Luis Alvarez, his son Walter, Frank Asaro, and Helen Michel.

The theory was initially met with skepticism, but over the years has become accepted as the primary explanation of the mass extinctions that took place sixty-five million years ago.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Great Mystery: What Killed the Dinosaurs? | date= 1995 | series = DinoBuzz | work = University of California Museum of Paleontology |url=https://ucmp.berkeley.edu/diapsids/extinction.html|access-date=2023-01-02}}</ref> Asaro himself felt that while mass extinction of many species was well-supported by plentiful fossil records, the smaller number of dinosaur fossils available worldwide made pinpointing cause of their extinction more difficult.  In the March 5, 2010, edition of ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'', an international panel of experts in geology, paleontology and related fields published the results of their exhaustive review of the data, ruling in favor of the asteroid theory.<ref>{{Cite web|author1= Lynn Yarris |date=9 March 2010|title=Alvarez Theory on Dinosaur Die-Out Upheld: Experts Find Asteroid Guilty of Killing the Dinosaurs | work= Berkeley Lab|url=https://newscenter.lbl.gov/2010/03/09/alvarez-theory-on-dinosaur/}}</ref>

==Legacy==

Minor planet [[4531 Asaro]] is named in his honor.<ref>{{cite book|chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/referenceworkentry/10.1007%2F978-3-540-29925-7_4469 |title=(4531) Asaro In: Dictionary of Minor Planet Names |chapter=(4531) Asaro |publisher=Springer |date=2003 |pages=390 |isbn=978-3-540-29925-7 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-29925-7_4469}}</ref>

In 2006, Asaro transferred archives of his work to the [[University of Missouri Research Reactor Center]] with the request that they transcribe these data and share them with the scientific community.  After more than a decade, a (nearly) comprehensive archive of the work of Asaro, Perlman, and Michel on the geochemistry of archaeological and geological samples was produced by Matthew T. Boulanger.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Boulanger |first=Matthew T. |date=2013 |title=Salvage Archaeometry: Lessons Learned from the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory Archaeometric Archives |url=http://onlinedigeditions.com/publication/?i=143555 |journal=The SAA Archaeological Record |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=14–19}}</ref> This archive was provided to the scientific community via the Digital Archaeological Record (tDAR).<ref>{{cite web | url = https://core.tdar.org/collection/7901/lawrence-berkeley-national-laboratory-lbnl-nuclear-archaeology-program-archives | work = The Digital Archaeological Record (tDAR) | author1= Matthew Boulanger| title = Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) Nuclear Archaeology Program Archives | date= 2018 | publisher= Arizona State University
}}</ref> The knowledge and experiences gained through working with these records has been used to recommend best practices to modern laboratories producing similar data to ensure that they remain useful into the future.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Citation |last=Boulanger |first=Matthew |chapter=Recycling Data: Working with Published and Unpublished Ceramic Compositional Data |date=8 December 2016 |chapter-url=https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/34668/chapter/295387439 |title=The Oxford Handbook of Archaeological Ceramic Analysis |pages=72–84 |editor-last=Hunt |editor-first=Alice |publisher=Oxford University Press |language=en |doi=10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199681532.013.6 |isbn=978-0-19-968153-2 |access-date=2022-10-07|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>
